question: A student writes def add(a, b): return a + b and calls add(2, 3). Using Python Crash Course for what happens at the Python level, and the RISC-V psABI and Winans's RISC-V Assembly Language Programming for how a function call works in RISC-V assembly, explain how arguments, the return value, and the return address are handled at each level. Treat these as two separate models; the scenario does not claim that Python compiles to RISC-V.

results.text:
Arguments and Parameters
       In the preceding greet_user() function, we defined greet_user() to require a
       value for the variable username. Once we called the function and gave it the
       information (a person’s name), it printed the right greeting.
         The variable username in the definition of greet_user() is an example of a
       parameter, a piece of information the function needs to do its job. The value
       'jesse' in greet_user('jesse') is an example of an argument. An argument
       is a piece of information that is passed from a function call to a function.
       When we call the function, we place the value we want the function to work
       with in parentheses. In this case the argument 'jesse' was passed to the
       function greet_user(), and the value was stored in the parameter username.

       Positional Arguments

       When you call a function, Python must match each argument in the function call with a parameter in the function definition. The simplest way to
       do this is based on the order of the arguments provided. Values matched
       up this way are called positional arguments.
         To see how this works, consider a function that displays information
       about pets. The function tells us what kind of animal each pet is and the
       pet’s name, as shown here:

return Values
       A function doesn’t always have to display its output directly. Instead, it can
       process some data and then return a value or set of values. The value the
       function returns is called a return value. The return statement takes a value
       from inside a function and sends it back to the line that called the function.
       Return values allow you to move much of your program’s grunt work into
       functions, which can simplify the body of your program.

results.text:
Chapter  2. Procedure  Calling  Convention

This chapter defines standard calling conventions, and describes how to pass parameters and
return values.

Functions must follow the register convention defined in calling convention: the contents of any
register without specifying it as an argument register in the calling convention are unspecified
upon entry, and the content of any register without specifying it as a return value register or callee-saved in the calling convention are unspecified upon exit, the contents of all callee-saved registers
must be restored to what was set on entry, and the contents of any fixed registers like gp and tp

never change,

         Calling convention for big-endian is NOT included in this specification yet, we
          intend to define that in future version of this specification.

2.1. Integer  Calling  Convention

The base integer calling convention provides eight argument registers, a0-a7, the first two of which
are also used to return values.

results.title: RISC-V ABIs Specification (version 1.0)
results.text:
Procedures must not rely upon the persistence of stack-allocated data whose addresses lie below
the stack pointer.

Registers s0-s11 shall be preserved across procedure calls. No floating-point registers, if present, are

preserved across calls. (This property changes when the integer calling convention is augmented by
the hardware floating-point calling convention.)

2.2. Hardware  Floating-point  Calling  Convention

The hardware floating-point calling convention adds eight floating-point argument registers, fa0-
fa7, the first two of which are also used to return values. Values are passed in floating-point

registers whenever possible, whether or not the integer registers have been exhausted.

The remainder of this section applies only to named arguments. Variadic arguments are passed
according to the integer calling convention.

results.title: RISC-V ABIs Specification (version 1.0)
results.text:
The ILP32E calling convention is designed to be usable with the RV32E ISA. This calling convention

is the same as the integer calling convention, except for the following differences. The stack pointer
need only be aligned to a 32-bit boundary. Registers x16-x31 do not participate in the calling
convention, so there are only six argument registers, a0-a5, only two callee-saved registers, s0-s1,
and only three temporaries, t0-t2.

If used with an ISA that has any of the registers x16-x31 and f0-f31, then these registers are

considered temporaries.

The ILP32E calling convention is not compatible with ISAs that have registers that require load and
store alignments of more than 32 bits. In particular, this calling convention must not be used with
the D ISA extension.

2.4. Named  ABIs

This specification defines the following named ABIs:

ILP32

  Integer calling-convention only, hardware floating-point calling convention is not used (i.e.
  ELFCLASS32 and EF_RISCV_FLOAT_ABI_SOFT).

results.text:
Storing the return address on both stacks preserves the call stack layout and the ABI,
          while also allowing for the detection of corruption of the return address on the
          regular stack. The prologue and epilogue of a non-leaf function that uses shadow
          stacks is as follows:

              function_entry:
                  addi sp,sp,-8 # push link register x1

                  sd x1,(sp)  # on regular stack
                  sspush x1  # push link register x1 on shadow stack
                  :
                 ld x1,(sp)  # pop link register x1 from regular stack
                  addi sp,sp,8
                  sspopchk x1 # fault if x1 not equal to shadow
                              # return address
                  ret

          This example illustrates the use of x1 register as the link register. Alternatively, the x5
          register may also be used as the link register.

The use of the compressed instruction C.SSPUSH x1 to push on the shadow stack is
 most efficient when the ABI uses x1 as the link register, as the link register may then
 be pushed without needing a register-to-register move in the function prologue. To
 use the compressed instruction C.SSPOPCHK x5, the function should pop the return

 address from regular stack into the alternate link register x5 and use the C.SSPOPCHK
 x5 to compare the return address to the shadow copy stored on the shadow stack.
 The function then uses C.JR x5 to jump to the return address.

The RVC standard extension for compressed instructions provides unconditional jump and conditional
branch instructions. The C.J and C.JAL instructions encode an offset in the immediate field of the
instruction and thus are not susceptible to control-flow subversion. The C.JR and C.JALR RVC
instructions perform an unconditional control transfer to the address in register rs1. The C.JALR
additionally writes the address of the instruction following the jump (pc+2) to the link register x1 and is

a procedure call. The C.JR is a return from procedure if rs1 is a conventional link register (i.e. x1 or x5);
else it is an indirect jump.

The term call is used to refer to a JAL or JALR instruction with a link register as destination, i.e., rd≠x0.
Conventionally, the link register is x1 or x5. A call using JAL or C.JAL is termed a direct call. A C.JALR
expands to JALR x1, 0(rs1) and is a call. A call using JALR or C.JALR is termed an indirect-call.

The term return is used to refer to a JALR instruction with rd=x0 and with rs1=x1 or rs1=x5. A C.JR
instruction expands to JALR x0, 0(rs1) and is a return if rs1=x1 or rs1=x5.

The term indirect-jump is used to refer to a JALR instruction with rd=x0 and where the rs1 is not x1 or x5
(i.e., not a return). A C.JR instruction where rs1 is not x1 or x5 (i.e., not a return) is an indirect-jump.

args.answer:
**Model 1 — the Python level (Python Crash Course)**

*Arguments.* In `def add(a, b):`, `a` and `b` are parameters — "a piece of information the function needs to do its job" — while the values in the call `add(2, 3)` are arguments, "a piece of information that is passed from a function call to a function"; when you call the function, "we place the value we want the function to work with in parentheses" [1]. With `add(2, 3)` the matching is positional: "Python must match each argument in the function call with a parameter in the function definition," and the simplest way is "based on the order of the arguments provided," so `2` binds to `a` and `3` to `b` [2]. (The book notes people often use "arguments" and "parameters" interchangeably.) Nothing about the call names a register or an address — the binding is name-to-value inside the function.

*Return value.* `return a + b` uses a return value: "The value the function returns is called a return value. The return statement takes a value from inside a function and sends it back to the line that called the function" [3]. Because a value comes back, the caller must give it a home: "When you call a function that returns a value, you need to provide a variable where the return value can be stored" — e.g. `musician = get_formatted_name('jimi', 'hendrix')` [4]. So `add(2, 3)` produces `5` at the calling line, and if you do not assign it, the value is simply unused. There is no return address at this level; the book's model is only "sends it back to the line that called the function" [3].

**Model 2 — the RISC-V level (psABI + Winans, with the ISA manual for the instructions)**

*Arguments.* The base integer calling convention "provides eight argument registers, a0-a7, the first two of which are also used to return values" [5]. A scalar of at most XLEN bits "are passed in a single argument register, or on the stack by value if none is available" [6]. So a two-integer call analogous to `add(2, 3)` puts the first value in `a0` (x10) and the second in `a1` (x11) — the caller loads them before the call. Winans's register table states the same roles: `x10-11 a0-1` are "Function arguments/return value," `x12-17 a2-7` "Function arguments" [14]. The body of the function would then be an `add rd, rs1, rs2` computing `rd ← rs1 + rs2` [18].

*Return value.* The result is left in `a0` (and `a1` for a second value), since the first two argument registers double as return registers [5]. The psABI register table marks `a0-a7` as *not* preserved across calls [7], and the general rule is that "the content of any register without specifying it as a return value register or callee-saved in the calling convention are unspecified upon exit" [5]; only `s0-s11` "shall be preserved across procedure calls" [8]. So the caller must grab the value out of `a0` immediately — the Python idea of "bind it to a variable" corresponds loosely to the caller copying `a0` somewhere durable.

*Return address.* The Base Integer ISA has "no dedicated stack pointer or subroutine return address link register"; "the standard software calling convention uses register x1 to hold the return address for a call, with register x5 available as an alternate link register. The standard calling convention uses register x2 as the stack pointer" [9]. `jal rd, offset` "Set[s] register rd to the address of the next instruction that would otherwise be executed (the address of the jal instruction + 4) and then jump[s] to the address given by the sum of the pc register and the imm_j value" [10] — so `jal ra, add` records where to come back to. Winans lists the assembler shorthands: `jal label` → `jal x1, label`, and `ret` → `jalr x0, 0(x1)` [11]; for a target out of range, the `call label` pseudoinstruction expands to `auipc x1, ...` followed by `jalr x1, ...` [12]. The ISA manual defines the terminology the same way: a "call" is a JAL/JALR with a link register as destination (`rd≠x0`, conventionally x1 or x5), and a "return" is a JALR with `rd=x0` and `rs1=x1` or `rs1=x5` [16].

*Why `ra` must be saved.* `x1 ra` is listed as *not* preserved across calls [7], so a function that itself makes another call (a non-leaf) must stash `ra` on the stack in its prologue and restore it in its epilogue; the 2025 manual shows exactly this shape: `addi sp,sp,-8`, `sd x1,(sp)` on entry, then `ld x1,(sp)`, `addi sp,sp,8`, `ret` on exit [15]. The stack "grows downwards (towards lower addresses) and the stack pointer shall be aligned to a 128-bit boundary upon procedure entry," with the first stack-passed argument at offset zero from `sp` [13]. Winans gives the rationale for the caller/callee split: classifying registers as "temporary" (not saved by any function that alters them) makes it "possible to carefully implement a function with less need to store register values on the stack" [17]. A leaf `add` like this one needs no save at all — it just computes into `a0` and executes `ret`.

**Two models, not a pipeline.** The Python account is about parameter/argument binding and a value sent back to the calling line [1][2][3]; the RISC-V account is about named registers, a link register, and stack discipline [5][7][9]. Nothing here claims `add(2, 3)` compiles to that sequence — Python integers are objects and the psABI rules apply to compiled RISC-V procedures, so the mapping is only an analogy. On the RISC-V side the 2019 manual lists the same roles with a "Saver" column (`x1 ra` → Caller, `a0–1` → "Function arguments/return values") [19]; it agrees with the psABI and the 2025 manual here, and in any case the 2025 manual controls.

There is no return-address notion at this level — only "sends it back to the line that called the function" [3].

**Model 2 — RISC-V assembly level (psABI + Winans, with the ISA manual for the instructions)**

*Arguments.* The base integer calling convention "provides eight argument registers, a0-a7, the first two of which are also used to return values" [5], and a scalar at most XLEN bits wide is "passed in a single argument register, or on the stack by value if none is available" [6]. So a two-integer call analogous to `add(2, 3)` places the first value in `a0` (x10) and the second in `a1` (x11) before the call; Winans's register table gives the same roles — `x10-11 a0-1` = "Function arguments/return value," `x12-17 a2-7` = "Function arguments," `x1 ra` = "Return address" [11]. The callee reads `a0`/`a1` and leaves the sum in `a0`.

*Return value.* The result is left in `a0` (and `a1` for a second value), because the first two argument registers double as return registers [5]. The psABI marks `a0-a7` as *not* preserved across calls, while `s0-s11` are callee-saved [7], and the general rule is that "the content of any register without specifying it as a return value register or callee-saved in the calling convention are unspecified upon exit" [5]. So the caller must move the value out of `a0` right away — the loose assembly counterpart of Python's "provide a variable where the return value can be stored" [4].

*Return address.* The Base Integer ISA has "no dedicated stack pointer or subroutine return address link register"; instead "the standard software calling convention uses register x1 to hold the return address for a call, with register x5 available as an alternate link register. The standard calling convention uses register x2 as the stack pointer" [8]. `jal rd, offset` "Set[s] register rd to the address of the next instruction that would otherwise be executed (the address of the jal instruction + 4) and then jump[s] to the address given by the sum of the pc register and the imm_j value" [9] — that is how the caller records where to come back to. Winans lists the assembler shorthands: `jal label` → `jal x1, label`, and `ret` → `jalr x0, 0(x1)` [10], i.e. the return jumps to the address held in `ra`.

*Saving `ra`.* Since `ra` is caller-saved/not preserved [7], a function that itself calls another function must stash it on the stack in its prologue and restore it in its epilogue; the 2025 manual shows exactly that shape — `addi sp,sp,-8` with `sd x1,(sp)` on entry, then `ld x1,(sp)`, `addi sp,sp,8`, `ret` on exit [12]. A leaf routine like this `add` needs no save: it reads `a0`/`a1`, writes `a0`, and executes `ret` [10].

**Two models, not a pipeline.** The Python account is about parameter/argument binding and a value sent back to the calling line [1][2][3]; the RISC-V account is about named registers, a link register, and stack discipline [5][7][8]. Nothing here claims `add(2, 3)` compiles into that instruction sequence — Python integers are objects, while the psABI rules govern compiled RISC-V procedures, so the correspondence is an analogy only. The 2019 manual lists the same register roles (with a Saver column: `x1 ra` → Caller, `a0–1` → "Function arguments/return values"), agreeing with the psABI; where versions differ, the 2025 manual controls.
